Every strong presentation starts long before you stand up. In this module you learn to study your audience, boil your idea down to one main message, build a simple opening, body and close with timings, and prepare your mind, your body and your venue so nerves do not take over.

Most weak presentations fail for one simple reason: the speaker tried to say everything. The audience leaves with a blur of facts and no clear idea of what to think or do. Strong speakers do the opposite. They decide **who** they are talking to, **what one idea** those people must remember, and **what they should do next**. Everything else is built on those three decisions.
A speaker aiming her message at a group of listeners
Before you plan a single slide, picture the exact people who will be in the room.
Four questions about your audience
**Who are they?** Women in your cooperative, a supermarket buyer, a grant panel, church members, a ward meeting. Note age range, language and how much they already know.

**What do they care about?** A buyer cares about price, steady supply and quality. A funder cares about impact and whether you can manage money. Neighbours care about their street, their children and their time.
**What do they already believe?** If they think the project failed last year, you must deal with that early, not hope nobody remembers.
**How much time and attention do they have?** A market association chairman may give you five minutes between other items. Plan for the time you will really get, not the time you hope for.

Also decide the language. In a mixed group you may present in English and repeat the main message and the action in Hausa, Igbo, Yoruba or Pidgin. If you use an interpreter, speak in short chunks of one or two sentences and give the interpreter your outline beforehand so key words are translated correctly.
Write your one main message

Your main message is the single sentence you want people to repeat to someone at home that evening. Write it before anything else. Keep it to 20 words or fewer, use plain words, and make it say something specific. "Our cooperative is doing well" is too vague. "Our cooperative can supply 200 loaves a day to your shop at a steady price from next month" is a message.
A useful test: imagine someone in the audience is asked, "What was her talk about?" If you cannot predict their one-line answer, your message is not clear yet. Rewrite it until you can.
Decide the action

A presentation should change something. Name the action you want: approve a budget, place a trial order, volunteer for Saturday, vote for the new drainage plan, sign up for a training. Make it small and clear enough that people can say yes today. "Support us" is weak. "Place a trial order of 50 packs this week" is strong.
Worked example: from a messy idea to one message

For example, Ngozi runs a small tailoring business in Enugu and has been invited to speak for 5 minutes at a women's business forum. Her first notes cover her life story, her machines, her prices, her training plans and a complaint about electricity.
Audience: about 40 women traders and two staff from a microfinance bank. They care about earning more and about who is reliable to work with.
She asks: what do I want from them? Answer: traders to order uniforms for their staff, and the bank staff to see her as a serious borrower.
First draft message (34 words) is too long and mixes two ideas.
Final message (17 words): "I make neat, durable staff uniforms in 10 working days, and I can take orders of 50 or more."
Action: "Give me your number after this session and I will bring fabric samples to your shop this week."
She cuts the electricity complaint and most of her life story, keeping one 30-second story about her first big order.
Her 5-minute talk now has one clear message, one action, and only the material that supports them.

Cut with courage

Once you have your message, go through every point you planned and ask: does this help the audience believe my message or take my action? If not, cut it or keep it in a back-up note for questions. Most speakers can cut a third of their first draft and the talk gets better, not worse.
The rule of three
Audiences remember three points much better than seven. Group your material into no more than three key points. If you have five, look for ones that can merge or move to your question notes.

A clear structure is a kindness to your audience. When people can sense where you are going, they relax and listen. The simplest structure, used by experienced speakers everywhere, has three parts: an **opening** that earns attention and states the message, a **body** of two or three key points, and a **close** that repeats the message and asks for action.

A time budget

A good rule is roughly 10 to 15 percent of your time for the opening, about 70 to 80 percent for the body, and about 10 percent for the close. Leave questions outside this budget unless the organiser tells you otherwise.

Openings that work
**A short, true story:** "Last March, a woman walked into my shop with a torn school uniform and 30 minutes before assembly." Keep it under 45 seconds.
**A question the audience cares about:** "How many of you have lost stock because the market flooded?"
**A surprising, checkable fact from your own work:** "In six months our group saved enough to buy two grinding machines."
**The problem, stated plainly:** "Our street has had no working drain since the rains began."

After the hook, state your main message and give a one-line map: "I will cover three things: what we produce, why buyers come back, and what a trial order looks like." Avoid opening with a long thank-you list or an apology such as "I am not a good speaker". Greet the chair briefly, then start.
Body patterns
**Problem, solution, benefit:** best for pitches and proposals.
**Past, present, future:** best for updates and reports.
**What, so what, now what:** what happened, why it matters, what we do next. Very good for short community updates.
**Three reasons:** best when you need people to agree with one decision.
Link the parts with transitions

Transitions are the short sentences that move the audience from one part to the next, such as "That is the product. Now, why do buyers come back?" They tell people a new point is starting and remind them where they are in your map. Plan one transition before each key point and before your close.
Closes that work

Signal the end ("To close..."), repeat your main message in almost the same words, then ask for the action clearly and say how. Never end with "That's all" or by fading out. Your last sentence is what people remember, so plan it word for word.

For example, Amina makes groundnut oil in Kano and has a 5-minute slot with the purchasing officer of a supermarket chain.

0:00 to 0:40 Opening. Hook: "Your customers ask for oil that smells fresh and does not foam." Message: "We supply clean, filtered groundnut oil in sealed bottles, every week, at a price you can plan with." Map: product, proof, trial order.
0:40 to 1:50 Point 1, the product: show one bottle, explain the filtering and sealing, state bottle sizes.
1:50 to 3:00 Point 2, proof: two shops already stock it; reorders every two weeks; customer comments shared with permission.
3:00 to 4:15 Point 3, the offer: trial order size, delivery day, payment terms, who to call.
4:15 to 5:00 Close: repeat message, ask: "Can we agree a trial order of 48 bottles for delivery next Tuesday?"

Manage nerves and get the room ready

Almost everyone feels nervous before speaking, including experienced speakers. A racing heart, dry mouth, shaky hands and a busy stomach are your body's normal stress response. It is getting you ready to perform. The goal is not to remove nerves completely but to keep them at a level where they give you energy instead of freezing you.
A woman sitting calmly with eyes closed
A minute of slow breathing before you stand up can steady your voice and hands.
Why preparation is the best cure

Most stage fright is fear of the unknown: forgetting what to say, technology failing, a hard question. Each of these can be reduced by preparation. When you have rehearsed your opening until you can say it without notes, checked the room and listed likely questions, there is much less left to fear.
A simple breathing routine
Sit or stand with both feet flat on the floor and drop your shoulders.
Breathe in slowly through your nose for a count of 4.
Breathe out slowly through your mouth for a count of 6, longer than the in-breath.
Repeat 5 to 6 times. A long out-breath helps the body calm down.
Take one sip of water, then say your first sentence quietly to yourself.
Reframe the feeling
Tell yourself "I am ready and alert" instead of "I am scared". The body feels much the same; the label changes how you use it.
Think of the talk as a conversation with the people in front of you, not a performance being judged.
Focus on what the audience needs from you. Attention on them leaves less attention for your own worries.
Find two or three friendly faces and speak to them first.
Get the room ready
Worked example: a venue check before a community meeting
For example, Funke will present a school-fees savings plan to about 60 parents in a church hall in Ibadan at 4 pm. She arrives at 3:15 pm.
Power: she asks where the sockets are and whether the generator will run. She has charged her laptop and phone fully and brought an extension cable.
Screen or none: the projector is unreliable, so she prints 10 copies of a one-page summary and plans to talk without slides if needed.
Sound: she tests the microphone at speaking volume from where she will stand and asks someone at the back if they can hear clearly.
Timing: she confirms with the chair that she has 10 minutes and when questions will be taken.
Safety: she makes sure cables are taped down or run along the wall so nobody trips, and notes the exits.
At 3:50 pm she does her breathing routine and says her opening line quietly twice.
When the generator fails at 4:05 pm, she is not thrown: she hands out the summary sheets and carries on without the microphone, speaking slowly and loudly.

Electricity and cables

Do not overload extension boxes with heaters, kettles and projectors together. Keep cables away from walkways or tape them down. Never handle plugs or sockets with wet hands, and if a socket sparks or smells of burning, stop using it and tell the organiser.
Privacy on screen

Before you present from your phone or laptop, turn off notifications or switch on Do Not Disturb so private WhatsApp messages do not pop up on the screen. Do not show photos of children, names with phone numbers, or members' savings balances unless everyone shown has agreed.
If nerves strike mid-talk

If your mind goes blank, pause, take a breath and look at your notes. A pause of three seconds feels long to you but normal to the audience. You can also repeat your last sentence or say "Let me come back to my main point" and restate your message. Keep a small card with your three key points in your hand as a safety net.

Canva works in a similar way: search for "Presentation", choose a simple template, replace the text and pictures with your own, and delete any template pages you do not need. Watch that templates do not tempt you into crowded pages full of decorations.
Rules for readable slides
**One idea per slide.** If a slide needs two headings, it should be two slides.
**Few words.** A short headline that states the point, plus a picture, number or up to three short lines.
**Big text.** Aim for at least about 28 point for body text and larger for headlines, so the back row can read it.
**Strong contrast.** Dark text on light, or light on dark. Avoid red on green and text over busy photos.
**Real photos of your own work** beat stock pictures. Ask permission before showing anyone's face.
**Simple charts.** One chart, few bars, and a headline that says what the chart shows.
Charts and pictures

If you show numbers, a simple bar chart is usually clearer than a table. In Google Slides you can insert a chart from the Insert menu; in Canva you can search for "chart" in the elements panel and type in your figures. Show only the numbers that support your point, label the bars clearly, and use the headline to say what the chart means, for example "Sales doubled after we started weekly delivery". Make sure every number on a slide is one you can explain and prove.
The 10/20/30 guide

Marketing writer Guy Kawasaki suggests a pitch of no more than 10 slides, 20 minutes, and no font smaller than 30 point. You do not need to follow it exactly, but it is a good check against long, crowded decks.
Worked example: turning a wordy slide into a clear one

New headline: "We deliver about 60 crates of eggs every week" (her real recent average).
Body: one photo of her crates ready for delivery, plus one line: "Same delivery day for the last 6 months."
The vaccines, staff and history move to speaker notes and to her question notes.
She checks the slide on her phone held at arm's length: the headline is still readable.

Your body: stand, move, gesture
**Stand:** feet about hip-width apart, weight even, knees soft. This stops swaying and rocking.
**Hands:** start with them loosely together at waist height, then let them gesture naturally. Avoid pockets, folded arms or gripping the table.
**Gestures:** keep them between waist and shoulders and match them to words, for example open palms for "all of us" or fingers for "three reasons".
**Move with purpose:** take a step or two when you change to a new point, then stand still while you make it.
**Face:** smile at the start and when appropriate. Let your face match your message; a serious issue deserves a serious face.
Eye contact across a room

Look at one person for about one full sentence or thought, then move to another person in a different part of the room. Cover left, centre and right, front and back. In a large hall, pick small groups instead of individuals. Avoid looking at the floor, the ceiling or your slides for long periods. Be aware that in some settings, long direct eye contact with elders may feel disrespectful, so soften your gaze and read the room.
Worked example: fixing delivery in one rehearsal
For example, Chioma records a 3-minute practice of her bakery pitch on her phone, propped on a shelf at eye level, then watches it back.
She counts filler words: 14 "em" sounds in 3 minutes, almost 5 a minute.
She notices she sways side to side and looks at her phone notes most of the time.
She marks 4 pauses in her notes and practises pausing silently instead of saying "em".
She plants her feet and practises her opening line looking at a spot on the wall.
Second recording: 4 filler words, no swaying, and she looks up for most of each sentence.
Two short recordings and three specific fixes cut her filler words from 14 to 4 and made her look far more confident.

Your face and hands also show how you feel about your own message. If you mention a sad event, slow down and lower your voice. If you announce good news, let your face light up. Audiences pick up emotion quickly, and a speaker who seems to believe her own message is far more persuasive than one who recites it.
Use the room and the microphone

Hold a handheld microphone about a fist's distance below your chin and keep it there when you turn your head. If there is no microphone, slow down and lift your volume; speaking more slowly makes you easier to hear than shouting quickly.

Dress for the audience and the setting, one step smarter than the people you are speaking to. Choose clothes and shoes you can stand comfortably in for the whole talk, and avoid jewellery that jangles near a microphone. When you feel physically comfortable, you think less about yourself and more about your audience.

Do not memorise every word. Memorise your opening, your key transitions and your close, and know your key points well enough to explain them in different words. Word-for-word memorising often makes people panic if they lose one sentence.
Asking for useful feedback
"How was it?" usually gets "It was fine". Instead, give your listener three specific questions before you start, so they know what to watch for.
What was my main message? (If they cannot say it, the message is not clear.)
Where did you lose interest or get confused?
What is one thing I should keep doing and one thing I should change?
When you get feedback, say thank you and write it down. Do not argue or explain. You can decide later what to use.
Sorting feedback

Not all feedback is equally important. Fix problems with the **message** and **structure** first, then **timing**, then **delivery**, then **slides**. A beautiful slide cannot save a talk whose message is unclear.
Worked example: acting on feedback for a cooperative update
For example, Esther is the secretary of a farmers' cooperative in Benue and will give a 6-minute update at the annual meeting. She rehearses in front of the treasurer and one member.
Feedback 1: "I thought the talk was about the new store, but it was about the loan." This is a message problem.
Feedback 2: "The list of meeting dates was boring." This is a structure problem.
Feedback 3: "You said 'em' a lot." This is a delivery problem.
She rewrites the message: "We repaid the loan in full and can now apply for a bigger one for a new store."
She replaces the list of dates with one line and moves the dates to a printed sheet.
Second rehearsal: both listeners repeat the message correctly and the talk runs 5 minutes 40 seconds.
By fixing the message first and the delivery last, the update became clear and fitted the 6-minute slot.

Keep a simple practice log: the date, the version you rehearsed, its length, the feedback you got and the change you made. After three or four entries you will see your own patterns, for example that you always run long in the middle point or always rush the close.

When you give feedback to others in a practice group, use the same kindness you hope to receive: start with one specific strength, give one specific change, and say how it would help the audience. "Your story about the flood was gripping; if you paused before the cost, it would stay with us" is far more useful than "Nice talk".

Meetings often run late, and your 10 minutes may become 4. Prepare a short version now: your opening, one sentence for each key point, and your close. Practise it once. If the chair asks you to be brief, you will be calm instead of rushed.

Evidence, questions and community meetings

A talk is only as strong as the trust people place in it. This module shows you how to support your message with honest evidence, handle questions and difficult moments calmly, and speak effectively at community and association meetings where decisions are made.
Support your message with honest evidence and stories
Choose the right kind of evidence for your audience
Present numbers so people understand and remember them
Tell a short story that supports your main point
Check every claim so you never overstate or mislead

People are persuaded by a mix of **facts** and **feelings**. A number shows that something is real and how big it is. A story makes people care. The strongest presentations use both, and they never claim more than the speaker can prove. One exaggerated figure that someone later checks can damage your reputation more than a weak talk ever would.

Making numbers clear
**Round sensibly:** say "about 240,000 naira" rather than "238,650 naira" unless the exact figure matters.
**Compare:** "That is about the cost of one bag of rice per member per year" helps people picture the amount.
**Use few numbers:** two or three key figures in a short talk. Put the full figures on a handout.
**Say where it comes from:** "From our sales book for January to June" makes the figure believable.
**Show change:** a before-and-after number is easier to remember than a single figure.

Match the evidence to the audience. A supermarket buyer wants proof of steady supply and consistent quality, so your delivery records and a sample matter most. A funder wants proof that money turns into results, so attendance registers, before-and-after figures and simple accounts matter most. Neighbours at a residents' meeting want to see the problem and the cost, so photos and a clear budget work best. One well-chosen piece of evidence for each key point is usually enough.
Short stories that work

A good presentation story is short, true and specific: one person, one moment, one change, told in under a minute. Use the shape **situation, problem, action, result**. Always ask permission before using someone's name or photo, and change details if the person could be embarrassed or put at risk.
Worked example: building evidence for a funder slide
For example, Zainab leads a women's group in Kaduna that trains young mothers in hairdressing. She is preparing a 10-minute presentation to a foundation that gives small training grants.
From her attendance register she counts 36 trainees who started in the past year and 29 who finished.
She works out the completion rate: 29 divided by 36 is about 0.81, so roughly 8 in 10 finished.

From follow-up phone calls she knows 17 of the 29 graduates are now earning from hairdressing. She says "17 of our 29 graduates told us they now earn from hairdressing", not "most of our women are now successful".
She adds one story, with permission: a graduate, for example Hauwa, who now runs a small salon corner in her compound.
She notes what she does not know: incomes were not recorded, so she makes no claim about earnings.
Her slide shows two checkable numbers, one story and an honest limit, which makes the funder more likely to trust everything else she says.

Each claim in your talk should travel this path, so the audience can see why they should believe it.
Never invent or stretch

Do not round 12 customers up to "dozens", call a plan a "result", or say a product is "NAFDAC approved" unless you hold the registration number. Claims about health benefits of food or cosmetics are especially risky. If you are not sure something is true, leave it out or say "we believe" and explain why.
Showing evidence on a phone or in print

You do not need a projector to show evidence. Keep photos of your records, certificates and products in one album on your phone so you can find them quickly. For a small group, a printed sheet with your two or three key numbers and a photo is often more effective than a screen, and people can take it home. Remove other people's private details, such as phone numbers or account balances, from any image you share.

Keep the source documents or photos on your phone for questions.

Honesty also means not hiding bad news. If sales dropped in the rainy season, say so and explain what you learned. Audiences, especially funders and members, trust speakers who report setbacks openly.

Handle questions, objections and difficult moments
Prepare for likely questions before the talk
Answer clearly using listen, pause, answer, check
Respond to hostile or off-topic questions calmly
Say "I don't know" honestly and follow up

Questions are good news: they show people are listening and thinking. They are also where buyers and funders test whether you really know your business. With preparation and a simple method, question time can become the strongest part of your presentation.
A person surrounded by question marks
Most questions can be predicted, so most answers can be prepared.
Prepare before the day

Write down the ten questions you would least like to be asked, then prepare a short answer to each. Common ones: "How much does it cost?", "What happens if you cannot deliver?", "Who else is doing this?", "How will you use the money?", "What went wrong last time?" Keep your evidence, price list and documents on your phone or on paper so you can show them.
A four-step method for any question
**Listen** to the whole question without interrupting. Look at the person.
**Pause** for a second or two. If the room is large, repeat or summarise the question so everyone hears it.
**Answer** briefly: the direct answer first, then one reason or example. Aim for about 30 to 60 seconds.
**Check:** "Does that answer your question?" Then move on.
Type of question
Example words
Clear and fair
Answer directly and briefly
"Yes, we deliver on Tuesdays and Fridays."
You don't know
Admit it and promise a follow-up
"I don't have that figure with me. I will send it to you by Friday."
Hostile or angry
Stay calm, find the real concern, answer that
"You are worried about the money. Here is exactly how it was spent."
Off-topic
Acknowledge and park it
"That's important; can we discuss it after the meeting?"
Long speech, no question
Thank them, pick out the question
"Thank you. I think the question is about timing, so..."
Keep answers short

Nervous speakers often answer a simple question with a five-minute speech, then lose the room. Give the direct answer in your first sentence, add one reason or example, and stop. If the person wants more, they will ask. A useful pattern for unplanned answers is **point, reason, example, point**: say your answer, give the reason, give one example, then repeat the answer in one line.
Handling objections from buyers and funders

An objection is a reason not to say yes, such as "Your price is too high". Treat it as a request for more information. First agree with the feeling, then give the facts: "I understand price matters. Our bottles are sealed and filtered, and we deliver free to your store, so your landed cost is close to the cheaper brands." Never criticise competitors by name; talk about what you do well.
Worked example: a hard question at a cooperative meeting
For example, Mercy is presenting the cooperative's yearly accounts to 50 members in Calabar. A member stands and says loudly: "Last year money went missing. Why should we trust these numbers?"
Mercy listens fully, does not interrupt, and nods to show she has heard.
She pauses and restates: "The question is whether these accounts can be trusted after last year's problem."
She answers in under a minute: two signatories are now required for every withdrawal, the bank statements are on the table for anyone to inspect, and two members checked the books last month.
She checks: "Does that answer your concern?" The member asks to see the statements.
Mercy invites him to look at them during the break and moves on with her presentation.
By staying calm, naming the real concern and pointing to evidence, Mercy turned a hostile challenge into a show of transparency.

Listen fully
Pause and restate
Answer briefly
Check and move on
Using the same four steps for every question keeps you calm and keeps answers short.
Questions in a group pitch or panel

If you present with a partner or team, agree beforehand who answers which kind of question, for example one person on product and one on money. When a question comes, the chair or lead speaker passes it on by name: "Amaka will take that one." Do not interrupt or correct each other in front of the audience; add a point afterwards only if something important was missed.
Getting questions started

If nobody asks anything, have one ready yourself: "A question I am often asked is..." This breaks the silence and often encourages others. In some settings people prefer to ask privately, so say you will stay behind afterwards.
If a meeting turns aggressive

If anyone becomes threatening, do not argue back or move closer. Ask the chair to manage the meeting, keep a clear path to the exit, and leave if you feel unsafe. Your safety matters more than finishing the talk.

Finally, end question time on your terms. When time is nearly up, say "I will take one more question", answer it, then repeat your main message and action. That way the last thing people hear is your message, not the last question.

Speak and report results at community meetings
Prepare a short, clear report for a community or association meeting
Follow the meeting's order and speak through the chair
Report money and progress in a way members can check
Propose a motion or decision people can vote on

Community meetings, such as residents' associations, market associations, cooperatives, church groups and school parent-teacher associations, are where many real decisions are made. Speaking well there can win support for a project, settle a dispute or get you elected. These meetings have their own customs, so a good speaker prepares for the setting as well as the content.
A group of people seated around a table in a meeting
In community meetings, short, clear reports and respectful manners carry great weight.
Know the meeting
**Get the agenda** (order of business) and find out when your item comes up and how much time you have.
**Greet according to custom:** acknowledge the chair, elders and any royal father or religious leader present, briefly.
**Speak through the chair:** say "Madam Chair" or "Mr Chairman" when you begin and when you answer questions.
**Wait to be recognised:** raise your hand and wait for the chair to call you.
**Language:** use the language most members understand; if needed, give key points in two languages.

Reporting money so members trust it

Members often care most about money. Present it in the simplest form: **opening balance, money received, money spent, closing balance**. Check that the numbers add up: opening balance plus received minus spent must equal closing balance. Mention where receipts and bank statements can be inspected. Use a printed sheet rather than reading many numbers aloud.
Worked example: a residents' association drainage report
For example, Grace is treasurer of a residents' association in Port Harcourt and has 5 minutes at the monthly meeting to report on the drainage fund. All figures are illustrative.
Purpose (30 sec): "Madam Chair, I am reporting on the drainage fund. In short: phase one is done and we need a decision on phase two."
What was done (1.5 min): 120 metres of drain cleared and repaired on two streets; photos passed round.
Money (1.5 min): opening balance ₦150,000, contributions received ₦450,000, spent ₦520,000, closing balance ₦80,000. Check: 150,000 + 450,000 minus 520,000 = 80,000.
Decision needed (1 min): phase two will cost about ₦400,000 by the contractor's quote. She proposes a levy of ₦5,000 per household from 80 households, which gives ₦400,000.
Close (30 sec): "I move that we approve a ₦5,000 levy for phase two, due by the end of next month. Receipts and the quote are on the table."
Her report is under 5 minutes, the money adds up and can be checked, and members have a clear motion to vote on.

Following the same order every month helps members follow quickly and compare reports over time.

Show photos rather than describing at length. Pass a phone round or print two or three pictures of the work done, such as the blocked drain before and the cleared drain after. Seeing the change helps members agree quickly and reduces argument about what was really achieved.
Proposing a motion

A motion is a clear proposal the meeting can vote on. Start with "I move that..." and include what, how much, who and by when. Ask a supporter beforehand if they will second it, if your group uses seconding.
Keep records

After the meeting, ask the secretary to record the decision in the minutes, and share a short summary on the association's WhatsApp group so members who were absent know what was agreed. Do not post individual members' payment status in the group without agreement; share that privately.
When there is disagreement

Community meetings can become heated, especially over money, land or leadership. Keep your voice level and slow, stick to facts and documents, and avoid blaming individuals in public. If an issue cannot be settled in the meeting, propose a small committee to look into it and report back by a set date. This shows respect for everyone's concern and keeps the meeting moving.
Measuring how your talk went

For a community report, success means: members understood the message, the decision was made, and fewer confused questions came up than last time. Note the number of questions, whether your motion passed and any follow-ups you promised. These simple notes help you improve your next report and give you real evidence of your progress as a speaker.

Pitch to buyers and funders, then keep growing

In this final module you apply everything to the presentations that can change your income: pitching your product to a buyer and pitching a project to a funder or lender. You also learn to present online and plan your next real speaking opportunities.
Pitch your product to a buyer
Research a buyer's needs before the meeting
Build a short pitch around what the buyer gains
Present your offer with clear price, quantity and terms
Ask for a specific trial order and agree next steps

A buyer pitch is a short business conversation, often 5 to 15 minutes, with a shop owner, supermarket purchasing officer, hotel manager, school or distributor. The buyer is not asking "Is this a nice product?" but "Will this sell, arrive on time, and make me money without problems?" Your pitch should answer those questions quickly and clearly.
A woman pitching an idea to a business person
A buyer pitch is a focused conversation about what the buyer gains.
Research the buyer first
Visit the shop or outlet. See which similar products they stock, the sizes, and roughly what they charge.
Notice gaps: empty shelf space, a product they often run out of, a size they do not carry.
Find out who makes buying decisions and when they are least busy.
Ask other suppliers, politely, about how the buyer pays: on delivery, after a week, or after sales.

Approx. time in 5 minutes

Keep the pitch conversational. Buyers often interrupt with questions; that is a good sign. Answer briefly and return to your outline. If the buyer is busy, offer the 60-second version: your product, the margin, the trial order you suggest.
Talk in the buyer's language

Buyers think in **margin** (the difference between what they pay you and what they sell for), **turnover** (how fast it sells) and **reliability**. Show the margin clearly. If you sell a jar to the shop for ₦1,200 and suggest a shelf price of ₦1,500, the shop earns ₦300 per jar, which is 25 percent of your price to them. Make sure your own price still covers your costs and profit before you offer it.

For example, Adaeze produces bottled zobo in Lagos and has 5 minutes with the manager of a busy neighbourhood supermarket. All prices are illustrative and approximate.

Hook (0:00): "I noticed your chiller has many soft drinks but no local drinks, and customers asked for zobo while I was here." Message: "We supply chilled, sealed zobo that sells fast and earns you a good margin."
Product (0:40): she hands over a cold 35 cl bottle, explains it is sealed, dated and labelled, and that it must stay refrigerated.
Proof (1:40): two nearby shops stock it and reorder weekly; she shows her delivery book on her phone.

Offer (2:40): price to the shop ₦400 per bottle, suggested shelf price ₦500, so ₦100 margin per bottle. Minimum order 24 bottles. Delivery Monday and Thursday. Payment on delivery for the first month.
Ask (4:15): "Can we start with a trial of 48 bottles this Monday? I will check on Thursday how they are selling."
The manager agrees to 24 bottles for a trial. Adaeze writes the order in her book, confirms the delivery day, and sends a WhatsApp message summarising the agreement.

Do not agree to quantities, prices or delivery days you cannot sustain. A buyer who is let down once may not buy again. If you are unsure, say "Let me confirm with my production schedule and call you by tomorrow."

Funders, such as foundations, development programmes, church or diaspora groups and microfinance lenders, hear many requests. They want to know three things: Is the problem real? Can this person or group deliver? Will the money be used well and produce results? Your pitch must answer all three with clear evidence, a sensible budget and a precise ask.

Loans are different from grants

A grant does not need to be paid back but usually needs detailed reports on how money was spent and what it achieved. A loan must be repaid with interest, so a lender focuses on your cash flow: can your business earn enough each month to make the repayments? In a loan pitch, show your recent sales records, your monthly costs and how the loan will increase income. Never borrow more than you can repay, and read every term before signing.

For example, Rukayat leads a women's group in Ilorin that wants a small grant to start a shea butter processing unit. All figures are illustrative and approximate.

Solution (1:30): a shared processing unit with a grinder and simple packaging so members can sell butter instead of nuts.
Evidence (3:30): over the past year the group trained 15 members in hygienic processing and sold small hand-made batches at a local market; she shows the sales book.

More meetings, trainings and pitches now happen online, through Google Meet, Zoom or WhatsApp video calls. The principles are the same as in a room: one message, a clear structure, honest evidence and good delivery. But the setup and the way you hold attention need extra care, because people can easily switch off or start doing something else.
A woman presenting to others on a video call
Online, your camera, light and sound are your stage.
Set up your space
**Camera at eye level:** prop your phone or laptop on books so the camera is level with your eyes, not looking up your nose.
**Light in front of you:** face a window or lamp. A bright window behind you turns you into a dark shape.
**Sound:** choose a quiet room, close the door, and use earphones with a microphone if you have them.
**Background:** a plain wall or tidy space. Check nothing private is visible.
**Power and data:** charge fully, keep a charger close, and check you have enough data or a stable Wi-Fi connection.
Presenting with shared slides
Join 10 minutes early to test sound, camera and screen sharing.
Close other apps and tabs, and switch on Do Not Disturb.
Share only the window or tab with your slides, not your whole screen, so private messages and files stay hidden.
Look at the camera when making key points, not at your own face on screen.
Stop sharing after the last slide so people can see you during questions.
Keep people with you

Online attention drops fast. Keep online talks shorter than in-room versions, change something every few minutes (a new slide, a question, a short poll) and use people's names: "Bisi, does that match what you see in your area?" Ask people to use the chat for questions and appoint a friend to read them out. If the connection is poor, turn off your video to save bandwidth and keep talking; voice matters more than picture.

1:30 to 9:00: three short points, each with one slide and a photo of a real notebook page; she pauses after each point for one chat question.
9:00 to 11:00: a quick task: members write today's sales in four columns and send a photo in the WhatsApp group.
11:00 to 12:00: close, repeat message, and remind them of the next session date.
Members with weak connections still have the PDF, and the quick task gives Lydia proof that they understood.

Why this matters
Do not try to say everything
Know who you are talking to
One clear action
Opening, body and close, on the clock
Most weak talks fail for one reason: the speaker tried to say everything. People leave with a blur of facts and no idea what to do.
Strong speakers decide three things first. Who they are talking to.
What one idea those people must remember.
And what they should do next.
Then they build a simple opening, body and close, with a time for each part.
Know your audience
Four questions before you write
Who are they?
What do they care about?
What do they already believe?
How much time and attention do they have?
First, who are they? Women in your cooperative, a supermarket buyer, a grant panel, a ward meeting.
What do they care about? A buyer cares about price, supply and quality. A funder cares about impact.
What do they already believe? If they think the project failed last year, deal with it early.
And how much time will you really get? A chairman may give you five minutes. Plan for that, not the time you hope for.
Vague or specific?
Too vague
Our cooperative is doing well
Support us
Clear
200 loaves a day, steady price
A trial order of 50 packs this week
Your main message is the one sentence you want people to repeat at home that evening. Keep it to 20 words or fewer. Our cooperative is doing well is too vague. Support us is a weak action.
Our cooperative can supply 200 loaves a day to your shop at a steady price from next month. That is a message.
And place a trial order of 50 packs this week is an action people can say yes to today.
Worked example
Ngozi finds her one message
Keep no more than three key points. Cut the rest.
Audience: about 40 traders and 2 bank staff
Want: uniform orders, and to look reliable
Message in 17 words, not 34
Action: give me your number today
Cut what does not support the message
For example, Ngozi runs a tailoring business in Enugu and has 5 minutes at a women's business forum. Her audience is about 40 traders and two bank staff.
She wants traders to order staff uniforms, and the bank staff to see her as a serious borrower.
Her first message was 34 words and mixed two ideas. Her final one is 17 words: I make neat, durable staff uniforms in 10 working days, and I can take orders of 50 or more.
Her action: give me your number after this session, and I will bring fabric samples to your shop this week.
She cuts her electricity complaint and most of her life story. Audiences remember three points much better than seven.
Opening, body and close
Never end with "That's all". Plan your last sentence.
Opening, 10 to 15 percent: hook, message, map
Body, 70 to 80 percent: two or three points
Close, about 10 percent: message and action
Give the opening about 10 to 15 percent of your time. Start with a hook, such as a short true story or a question they care about. Then state your message and a one-line map.
The body gets about 70 to 80 percent. Choose a pattern, such as problem, solution, benefit for a pitch, or what, so what, now what for a short update.
The close gets about 10 percent. Say to close, repeat your message, and ask for the action clearly. In a 5-minute talk, that is about 45 seconds each for opening and close.
Calm your nerves
A one-minute breathing routine
Nerves are normal. Manage them, do not fight them.
Feet flat, shoulders down
Breathe in through your nose for 4
Breathe out through your mouth for 6
Repeat 5 to 6 times
Sip water, say your first line quietly
A racing heart and dry mouth are your body's normal stress response. It is getting you ready.
Stand with both feet flat and drop your shoulders.
Breathe out through your mouth for a count of 6. The long out-breath helps your body calm down.
Repeat this 5 to 6 times.
Take one sip of water, and say your first sentence quietly to yourself. If your mind goes blank mid-talk, pause, breathe, and look at your key-point card.
Safety and privacy
Cables taped down, exits known
Phone on Do Not Disturb
Water and a printed back-up
Arrive 30 to 45 minutes early. Know your opening by heart. Charge your devices and save your files offline. Test the sound from where you will stand.
Tape cables down so nobody trips. Never overload extension boxes, never touch plugs with wet hands, and if a socket sparks, stop and tell the organiser.
Turn on Do Not Disturb so private messages do not pop up on screen, and never show children or savings balances without consent. Bring water and a printed back-up in case the power fails.

One small, clear action
No more than three key points
Breathe in for 4, out for 6

Fix the big things first
Slides should help people understand and remember. They are not your script. Many community talks work better with no slides at all, or one printed sheet.
The same words can sound weak or powerful. Your voice and body are tools you can train.
Reading your notes silently is not rehearsal. Say the words aloud, standing, with a timer.
And when feedback comes, fix the big things before the small things.
Readable slides
Rules for slides people can read
One idea per slide
A headline that states the point
Big text: about 28 point or more
Strong contrast, no busy backgrounds
Real photos, with permission
Keep an offline PDF copy
Use Google Slides or Canva, both free on a phone. One idea per slide. If a slide needs two headings, make two slides.
Give each slide a headline that states the point, plus one picture, number, or up to three short lines. Put your script in the speaker notes.
Make the text big, about 28 point or more, so the back row can read it.
Use dark text on light, or light on dark. Avoid text over busy photos.
Real photos of your own work beat stock pictures. Ask permission before showing anyone's face.
And download a PDF copy and keep it on your phone, so you can present even with a poor network.
Worked example
Halima's crowded slide, fixed
Crowded
Vague title: Our Farm
Clear
About 60 crates of eggs every week
One photo of crates ready to go
Same delivery day for 6 months
For example, Halima runs a poultry farm near Abuja. Her first slide was titled Our Farm, with eight bullet points about history, birds, feed, vaccines, staff and plans.
She asked: what is the one point? That the farm delivers reliably. Her new headline: we deliver about 60 crates of eggs every week. One photo, one line, and the rest moved to her notes.
Your voice
Pace, volume and pauses
Especially in the first minute and on key points. Nerves make you rush.
Speak to the person at the back. Do not drop your volume at the end of sentences.
Pause before and after your main message and key numbers. Silence makes the number land.
Slow down, especially in the first minute and on key points. Nerves make most of us rush.
Speak to the person at the back of the room, and keep your volume up to the end of each sentence.
And pause before and after your key number. Mark a slash in your notes where you will pause. For example: we saved, pause, two hundred and forty thousand naira, pause, in six months.
Your body
Stand, gesture and look up
Your accent is fine. Clarity comes from pace and pauses.
Feet hip-width apart, weight even
Hands loose, gestures waist to shoulder
Move only when you change point
Eye contact: one thought, then move on
Stand with your feet about hip-width apart and your weight even. This stops swaying.
Keep your hands loose, and let them gesture between waist and shoulders. Avoid pockets and folded arms.
Take a step or two when you change to a new point, then stand still while you make it.
Look at one person for one full thought, then move to another part of the room. With elders, soften your gaze and read the room. And you do not need to change your accent.
Chioma's two-take drill
Record 3 minutes, phone at eye level
Count: 14 em sounds, swaying
Mark 4 pauses in her notes
Plant her feet, look up
Second take: 4 fillers, no swaying
For example, Chioma records a 3-minute practice of her bakery pitch, with her phone on a shelf at eye level.
Watching it back, she counts 14 em sounds, and sees she sways and looks down at her notes.
She marks 4 pauses, and practises pausing silently instead of saying em.
She plants her feet and practises her opening line looking up.
Her second recording has only 4 filler words and no swaying.
Feedback
Ask three questions, fix in order
What was my main message?
Where did you lose interest?
Fix: message, structure, timing, delivery, slides
How was it, usually gets, it was fine. So give your listener three questions before you start.
What was my main message? If they cannot say it, your message is not clear.
And what is one thing to keep doing, and one thing to change? Say thank you, write it down, and do not argue.
Then fix in this order: message, structure, timing, delivery, and slides last. A beautiful slide cannot save an unclear message. Prepare a short version too, in case your 10 minutes become 4.

One idea per slide; keep an offline PDF
Slow down, project, pause before key points
Plant your feet; move with purpose
Rehearse aloud, standing, with a timer

For example, Zainab leads a women's group in Kaduna that trains young mothers in hairdressing. She is pitching to a foundation. From her register, 36 trainees started and 29 finished. That is roughly 8 in 10.

Any question
Not sure? Say "I don't know", and follow up by a set date.
Listen to the whole question
Pause, and restate it for the room
Answer briefly: 30 to 60 seconds
Check: does that answer your question?
Before the day, write down the ten questions you would least like to be asked, and prepare a short answer to each. Then use four steps.
Listen to the whole question without interrupting.
Pause for a second or two. In a large room, restate the question so everyone hears it.
Answer briefly. The direct answer first, then one reason or example. Nervous speakers often give a five-minute speech and lose the room.
Then check, does that answer your question, and move on. If you do not know, say so: I will send it to you by Friday.

Stay calm, name the real concern, point to evidence.
Listens fully and nods
Restates the real concern
Answers with facts in under a minute
Checks, then moves on
For example, Mercy presents yearly accounts to 50 members in Calabar. A man stands and shouts: last year money went missing. Why should we trust these numbers?
Mercy listens fully, without interrupting.
She restates: the question is whether these accounts can be trusted after last year's problem.
In under a minute she explains: two signatories are now needed for every withdrawal, the bank statements are on the table, and two members checked the books.
She checks, invites him to see the statements at the break, and moves on.

A report in five parts
Purpose and main message
Money: received, spent, balance
Close: repeat the decision, invite questions

First, your purpose and main message.
What was done since the last meeting. Pass round photos rather than describing at length.
The money, in its simplest form.
Next steps, and the decision you need.
Then close by repeating the decision, and invite questions through the chair.

Opening balance
Contributions received (add)
Spent (take away)
Figures are illustrative.

Decision and safety
End with a motion, keep it safe
If a meeting turns threatening, your safety comes first.
Start with "I move that..."
Say what, how much, who and by when
Never post members' payments in the group

First, visit the shop. See what similar products they stock, what they charge, and what is missing from the shelf.
Open with a need you noticed in their shop, then your one-line offer.
Show the product. Let them see, touch or taste it, and give sizes and packaging.
Give proof: who already buys, and how often they reorder.
Make a clear offer: price to them, suggested shelf price, minimum order, delivery days and payment terms.
Then ask for a specific trial order. If you are unsure you can supply it, say: let me confirm with my production schedule and call you by tomorrow.

Funding pitch
Six parts funders check
Problem: what is wrong, how do you know?
Solution: what you will do
Evidence: what you have already done
Plan and budget: what the money buys
Ask: how much, for what, what next
A funding pitch has six parts. The problem, and how you know it is real. Then your solution.
Your evidence. For example, Rukayat's shea group in Ilorin had already trained 15 members and sold small batches, and she showed the sales book.
Your plan and budget. Base each line on real quotes, tie it to a result, and show what you contribute yourself.
Your team, and how money will be tracked: two signatories, and regular reports with photos and sales records.
And a precise ask. Rukayat asked for 900,000 naira to set up the unit within three months, and offered to send the full proposal that week.
Protect your money
Loans, grants and scams
No repayment, but careful reports on how money was spent and what it achieved.
Repaid with interest. Show your cash flow. Never borrow more than you can repay.
Never pay a fee to release a grant. Never share your PIN or OTP. Check the official website.
A grant does not need to be paid back, but it usually needs detailed reports.
A loan must be repaid with interest, so a lender looks at your cash flow. Never borrow more than you can repay, and read every term before signing.
Be careful of anyone who asks for a fee to release a grant, or promises guaranteed funding on social media. Real funders publish how to apply. Never share your bank PIN or OTP.

Online, prop your phone so the camera is at eye level. Face a window or lamp, never with a bright window behind you. Choose a quiet room.
Share only the window with your slides, so private messages stay hidden, and switch on Do Not Disturb. Keep it short and use people's names.
Send a PDF summary the day before, so members with poor connections still get the content.

After each talk, write in your speaker log: your message, the time you used, the result, and one thing to keep and one to change.
